summary: We built FireX for the NASA Space Apps Challenge—an interactive 3D map that brings together and cleans up years of active fire data across India from 2022 to 2026. The main headache with satellite data is that different sensors catch fires differently. To fix that, FireX cross-calibrates NASA's MODIS (1km) and VIIRS (375m) feeds using pixel-area math so everything lines up on the same page. The app lets you explore a sleek 3D globe where you can zoom smoothly from a national overview right down to individual states and districts, scrub through a seasonal time-lapse player, and check out detailed stats. It’s built to actually be useful: it gives local communities a heads-up on seasonal burning cycles, helps researchers dig into exact burn sizes and thermal power, and gives forest departments and emergency crews the clear insights they need to dispatch help where it's needed most. Ultimately, it’s about turning heavy, complicated NASA space telemetry into something clean, fast, and genuinely impactful.
details:
When we started building FireX for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we wanted to tackle a real headache with satellite data: different sensors see the world differently. To fix that, we built an interactive 3D geospatial dashboard that harmonizes NASA's MODIS (1km) and VIIRS (375m) fire feeds across India from 2022 to 2026, bringing everything onto a single, reliable scale using pixel-area normalization.

We wanted the app to feel like a modern mission-control tool. Users get a sleek 3D globe where they can smoothly zoom from a national view (L1) down to individual states (L2) and districts (L3), scrub through a seasonal time-lapse player, and click districts to check out burn areas (km2) and sensor breakdowns. On the tech side, we put it together using react-globe.gl, Three.js, custom Geo JSON mapping, and a Python-powered data pipeline.

Beyond the code, we really focused on making it useful. FireX gives local communities early visibility into regional burning cycles, helps researchers analyze precise thermal data, and gives forest departments and emergency responders clear insights to track fire intensity and allocate resources where they're needed most. It's all about turning heavy satellite telemetry into something fast, clean, and genuinely helpful.
